title: Fire on the Mountain
summary: Two chords, B and A, round and round. Perfect for drilling barre changes, then breaking out of them with triads and B mixolydian fills.
notes: Chord progression and practice parts only. The fills here are original exercises in the style, not transcriptions.

lessons.title: Lock in the barre change
lessons.goal: Switch B to A on beat one without the strumming hand stopping.
body: B is an A-shape barre at the 2nd fret, root on the A string. A is an E-shape barre at the 5th fret, root on the low E string. Your hand slides up three frets and the shape flips.
Keep the strumming hand moving down and up the whole time, even through the change. The pattern is down, down-up, up-down-up.
steps: Play along with the rhythm guitar part at 80 bpm until the change feels boring.
Mute the rhythm guitar and keep going on your own.
Push the tempo toward 100, then the record's 116.

lessons.title: Same two chords, three places on the neck
lessons.goal: Play B and A as three-string triads at the 2nd, 7th and 12th frets.
body: A triad is just the root, third and fifth. On the top three strings each shape is one note per string, so it's small, quick and easy to move.
Every chord has three triad shapes on a string set: root on the bottom, third on the bottom, or fifth on the bottom. Switch the fretboard to Triads to see all of them for whichever chord is playing.
steps: Pick the "Triads, 7th fret" variation and play along.
Try the 2nd-fret and 12th-fret versions. Notice B and A are always the same shape, two frets apart.
Mix them: one bar up high, one bar low. That's how rhythm players stay interesting on a two-chord vamp.

lessons.title: Sixteenth-note strumming
lessons.goal: Keep a constant sixteenth-note arm motion and choose which strokes hit.
body: Your arm swings down-up four times per beat. Some strokes hit the strings, some miss on purpose, and the x strokes are muted chucks where the fretting hand relaxes off the strings.
Lowercase letters in the pattern are lighter strokes. Capitals are accents.
steps: Start at 70 bpm with the "Sixteenth funk" variation playing.
Mute rhythm guitar and copy it.
Change one stroke at a time to invent your own pattern.

lessons.title: Map B mixolydian
lessons.goal: Play B mixolydian in all five positions.
body: Mixolydian is the major scale with the seventh lowered one fret. In B that turns A# into A, which is exactly why the A chord fits.
Position 1 starts on the B at the 7th fret of the low E string. If you already know the major scale shape there, just flatten each seventh.
steps: Play position 1 up and down along with the groove, one note per beat.
Step through positions 2 to 5 and find where each one overlaps the last.
Roots are amber, so use them as landmarks.

lessons.title: Aim at the chord tones
lessons.goal: Make melodies that follow the chords by landing on their thirds.
body: Over B, the third is D#. Over A, it's C#. Landing on those notes as the chord changes makes a melody sound like it belongs.
The "Mixolydian fills" part does exactly that: it ends the B bar on D# and the A bar on C#.
steps: Listen to the fills a few times with the fretboard on Chord tones.
Mute the lead part and play the fills yourself.
Now improvise, but promise to land on the teal third each time the chord changes.

lessons.title: Melodies from inside the chord shape
lessons.goal: Play a melody without letting go of the barre shapes.
body: Flatpickers who seem to improvise endlessly, the way David Rawlings does, are mostly not running scales up and down. They hold a chord shape and pick the melody out of the notes under their fingers, adding a neighbour note or a hammer-on for movement.

Over B, hold the A-shape barre at the 2nd fret: the melody uses B, D# and F# from the shape plus C# with your second finger. Over A, hold the E-shape at the 5th fret and borrow D on the G string's 7th fret before falling back to C#.
steps: Fret the B chord and play the melody without lifting the barre.
Same for A at the 5th fret. Notice your hand never really moves.
Make up your own: one note from the shape per beat, then add one neighbour note per bar.
Play it with your eyes closed. Knowing where you are from the shape is what lets players look away from the neck.

lessons.title: Write your own fill
lessons.goal: Capture a two-bar fill and save it as a new variation.
body: Open Capture, pick the Vamp section, and record a phrase with a MIDI keyboard or by tapping the fretboard.
Save it to the song and it shows up as a new lead variation you can loop and print.
steps: Record two bars over B then A.
Keep the one you like and download the song file to commit it.

lessons.title: Two hands, two jobs
lessons.goal: Left hand plays roots on beats 1 and 3 while the right hand stabs the offbeats.
body: Splitting the work is the first step of two-handed playing. The left hand is the bass player: B or A, low and steady. The right hand is the rhythm guitar: a three-note chord on every 'and'.
Right hand B is B–D#–F#, A is A–C#–E. Every finger moves down one step at the change.
steps: Watch the keyboard on Part and play only the left hand along with the track.
Now only the right hand.
Mute the keys and put them together at 70 bpm.

lessons.title: Smaller moves between chords
lessons.goal: Find an A chord shape that's closer to your B.
body: Instead of sliding the whole B triad down, try A in first inversion: C#–E–A. From B–D#–F#, your thumb moves B to C#, and the other fingers barely move.
Turn on Chord tones to see every B or A note across the keyboard, and pick the nearest ones.
steps: With Chord tones on, find three different ways to play A within reach of your B.
Pick the one that moves least and use it with the Two hands part.

lessons.title: Melody over a left-hand pulse
lessons.goal: Keep the left hand on roots while the right hand plays a mixolydian line.
body: The right hand line climbs F#–G#–A–B over the B chord and steps down to C# for the A chord, landing on the third. The left hand just plays the root on beat one.
steps: Play the melody alone from the Sheet page.
Add the left hand: one note per bar.
Mute keys and play both along with the band.

lessons.title: Anatomy of the groove
lessons.goal: Hear what each drum is doing on its own.
body: Kick on 1 and the 'and' of 2 pushes the song forward; snare on 2 and 4 is the backbeat; the hi-hat keeps eighths. The two quiet 'o' notes are ghost snares, which give it swing without getting louder.
steps: Solo the drums and follow each lane on the pads.
Switch between Groove, Half-time and Four on the floor and notice how the same tempo feels faster or slower.

lessons.title: A two-bar phrase with a fill
lessons.goal: Make bar two different from bar one so the loop breathes.
body: A fill is a small change at the end of a phrase that tells the band something is coming. Here the hats drop out, the snare doubles up and two toms lead back to the one.
Open Capture, pick Drums, set the length to 2 bars and make your own version. Change one lane at a time.
steps: Listen to Groove with a fill.
In Capture, start from Groove, set 2 bars, and change only the last two beats of bar two.
Save it and loop it with the band.

lessons.title: A warm organ comp on the FM-1
lessons.goal: Build a sound for the offbeat stabs.
body: The keys part here works best with a soft organ-like tone. In FM terms: a sine carrier with a modulator at the same frequency (1:1 ratio), a low modulation amount, a fast attack and full sustain. Raise the modulation for more bite in the Jam.
Mute the keys part and play the stabs on your synth so you hear your sound in the band.
steps: Load Organ in the FM lab (or start from a plain sine on your synth) and add modulation slowly until it sounds like an organ.
Shorten the release so the stabs stay tight.
Mute keys and play the offbeat stabs on your synth or the lab’s keys.
